title: wait() vs task.wait()
summary: Legacy wait() rounds up to ~1/30s steps, caps at 10 minutes, and returns three values. task.wait() is precise, has no cap, and returns elapsed time. New code should always use task.wait.

explanation.whatItIs: Two generations of the same idea. The old one is quantized to the frame scheduler's coarsest step and behaves oddly; the new one honors your number.
explanation.whyItExists: wait() predates the task scheduler rework; keeping it avoids breaking ancient games, but it shouldn't ship in new ones.
symptoms: Old tutorials everywhere using bare wait()
explanation.fix: Replace wait(x) with task.wait(x); replace wait() with task.wait() (yields a single frame); replace spawn/delay with task.spawn/task.delay.
tips: task.wait returns ELAPSED time — usually more useful than the legacy triple
task library functions also come in pairs: task.spawn/task.delay/task.defer
commonMistakes: Copying tutorial code with wait()/spawn()/delay() verbatim
Assuming wait() precision for rhythm/cooldown mechanics

examples.title: Side by side
examples.code:
-- ❌ legacy:
wait(0.5)                    -- may sleep coarser than 0.5
local s = spawn(function() end)

-- ✅ modern:
task.wait(0.5)               -- honors 0.5s
local elapsed = task.wait(1) -- returns actual elapsed
local thread = task.spawn(function() end)
